lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: Achilles, the things you said to Odysseus the other day about death — they were unworthy of your teachers, Chiron and Phoenix both. I heard you when you said you'd rather be a servant on some poor man's farm than rule over all the dead. That might be something for a cowardly Phrygian to say, someone too attached to life. But for the son of Peleus, the most daring of all heroes, to think so little of himself... it's shameful. It goes against everything you accomplished in life. You could have ruled for years in Phthia without glory, but you chose death with a good name instead.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: Son of Nestor, back then I hadn't experienced this place yet. I didn't know which was better, so I preferred that wretched little glory to life. Now I understand — glory is useless here, even if they sing about it up there. Among the dead, everyone has the same status. That beauty and strength of mine aren't here. We all lie under the same darkness, no different from one another. The Trojan dead don't fear me, the Achaean ones don't wait on me. There's perfect equality of speech — a dead man is the same whether he was bad or good. That's what bothers me. I wish I were still alive and serving.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: What can anyone do, Achilles? That's how nature arranged it — everyone dies. So we have to stick to the rules and not get upset about what's been set. Besides, look how many of your companions are here with us. Odysseus will be here soon enough. Sharing the experience helps, and knowing you're not the only one. You see Heracles and Meleager and those other great men — I don't think they'd take the chance to go back and serve some poor man with nothing.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: Your advice is well-meant, but the memories of life still pain me. And I think they pain each of you too. If you won't admit it, you're worse off for suffering in silence.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: No, we're better for it, Achilles. We see that talking about it does no good. We've decided to be quiet, to bear it and endure, so we don't become a joke like you, wishing for the impossible.
